questions.enonce_markdown: Show that a root of the equation $x^3 + x^2 + 3x - 2 = 0$ lies in the interval $-1 < x < 1$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $g(x) = x^3 + x^2 + 3x - 2$. This is a polynomial, so $g$ is continuous on $[-1, 1]$.

$$g(-1) = -1 + 1 - 3 - 2 = -5 < 0, \qquad g(1) = 1 + 1 + 3 - 2 = 3 > 0.$$

$g(-1)$ and $g(1)$ have opposite signs. By the intermediate value theorem there is at least one value $c$ with $-1 < c < 1$ such that $g(c) = 0$. So a root of the equation lies in the interval $-1 < x < 1$. $\blacksquare$

(For information, $g(0) = -2 < 0$ and $g(1) = 3 > 0$ already narrow the root to $0 < x < 1$; $g(0.5) = -0.125 < 0$ and $g(0.6) = 0.376 > 0$ place it near $x \approx 0.53$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
A line $L$ and a plane $\pi$ have equations
$$L:\ \mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} + \lambda(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}), \qquad \pi:\ x - 2y + 2z = 3.$$
Show that the point $P(2, -2, 3)$ lies on $L$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A point lies on $L$ if its position vector equals $3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} + \lambda(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k})$ for some single value of $\lambda$. Component by component, with $P = (2, -2, 3)$:

$$\mathbf{i}:\ 3 + \lambda = 2 \Rightarrow \lambda = -1; \qquad \mathbf{j}:\ -1 + \lambda = -2 \Rightarrow \lambda = -1; \qquad \mathbf{k}:\ 2 - \lambda = 3 \Rightarrow \lambda = -1.$$

All three components give the same value $\lambda = -1$, so $P(2, -2, 3)$ lies on $L$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown:
A line $L$ and a plane $\pi$ have equations
$$L:\ \mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} + \lambda(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}), \qquad \pi:\ x - 2y + 2z = 3.$$
Find the position vector of the point of intersection of $L$ and $\pi$. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A general point of $L$ is $(x, y, z) = (3 + \lambda,\ -1 + \lambda,\ 2 - \lambda)$. It lies on $\pi$ when it satisfies $x - 2y + 2z = 3$:

$$(3 + \lambda) - 2(-1 + \lambda) + 2(2 - \lambda) = 3$$
$$3 + \lambda + 2 - 2\lambda + 4 - 2\lambda = 3$$
$$9 - 3\lambda = 3 \Longrightarrow \lambda = 2.$$

Substituting $\lambda = 2$: $(x, y, z) = (3 + 2,\ -1 + 2,\ 2 - 2) = (5, 1, 0)$.

Check in $\pi$: $5 - 2(1) + 2(0) = 3$. Correct.

$$\boxed{\mathbf{r} = 5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
A line $L$ and a plane $\pi$ have equations
$$L:\ \mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} + \lambda(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}), \qquad \pi:\ x - 2y + 2z = 3.$$
Determine the sine of the angle between $L$ and $\pi$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The direction vector of $L$ is $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}$ and a normal vector to $\pi$ is $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$.

The angle $\theta$ between the line and the plane is the complement of the angle between $\mathbf{d}$ and $\mathbf{n}$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}|\,|\mathbf{n}|}$.

$$\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n} = (1)(1) + (1)(-2) + (-1)(2) = 1 - 2 - 2 = -3, \qquad |\mathbf{d}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt3, \qquad |\mathbf{n}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3.$$

$$\sin\theta = \frac{|-3|}{\sqrt3\times 3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}.$$

$$\boxed{\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3} \approx 0.577}$$

(So $\theta \approx 35.3^\circ$.)
